# Introduction

The proliferation of Next-Generation Sequencing (NGS) tools for predicting 
Copy Number Aberrations (CNAs) has led to a significant data integration 
challenge in bioinformatics. Each application, while serving the same core purpose, 
generates results in a unique output format, often spread across multiple files. 
Furthermore, the specific metrics and fields reported—such as segment start/end positions, 
log-ratio values, and associated p-values—are frequently named differently or 
are not uniformly present across all tool outputs. 
This lack of standardization creates substantial overhead for researchers, 
who must write custom parsing scripts for every new tool, leading to complex 
and error-prone downstream analysis. It is exceptionally difficult to compare 
results across different methods, integrate them into common analysis pipelines, 
or use them with existing visualization and interpretation software, 
even when using semi-standard formats like SEG or VCF which haven't achieved universal adoption.

A dedicated package capable of reading the diverse outputs of CNA prediction tools 
and translating them into a single, common, standardized format is crucial for 
streamlining genomic data analysis. Such a package would significantly reduce 
the need for custom scripting, allowing researchers to focus on biological 
interpretation rather than data wrangling. By providing a consistent data 
structure, it would immediately enable method comparison, consensus calling, 
and seamless integration with downstream analysis and visualization tools, 
irrespective of the initial prediction method. This unified approach promotes 
reproducibility and interoperability across different studies and laboratories, 
ultimately accelerating the pace of discovery in cancer genomics and other fields 
relying on CNA analysis.

`cnvstrmliner` is a package that tries to assume the role of this middle layer
that is capable of parsing multiple output formats and provide a single uniform one 
using standard Bioconductor objects.
Furthermore, some additional functionality is added to facilitate the comparisons and 
QC.

## The example dataset

All the examples below use a single sample, **`BRCA_XX_01_pur30_T`**, distributed with
the package under `extdata/example_CNV/BRCA_XX_01`. It is a simulated breast tumour with
a matched normal, diluted to a nominal 30% tumour purity and processed through five CNV
callers. This vignette uses the FACETS output only; the other four appear in the
*Parsing CNV caller outputs* vignette.

This is a **whole-exome (WES)** sample, captured with the Agilent SureSelect Human All
Exon V6 kit. That matters throughout: the callers only see the captured intervals, so
segment boundaries are constrained to the target regions, marker counts per segment are
far lower than in WGS, and the off-target genome is simply not observed. The coordinates
of the capture kit are shipped alongside the caller output and are used below wherever a
common set of genomic intervals is needed.

```{r datadir}
root <- system.file("extdata/example_CNV/BRCA_XX_01", package = "cnvstrmliner")
list.dirs(root, recursive = FALSE, full.names = FALSE)

# coordinates of the capture kit used for this sample
bed.file <- file.path(root, "S07604514_Regions_v6_hg38_Targets.bed.gz")
```

The companion vignette *Parsing CNV caller outputs* concentrates on the parsers and on
plotting; this one follows a single sample through a whole analysis: load, summarise,
annotate, export, and QC.

# The `cnvstrml` object

The package can parse and load data from various CNV callers; `getSupportedMethods()`
lists the ones currently supported. For each of them `loadCNV()` accepts the output files
together with a `cnv.method` argument, and a caller-specific `parse<CALLER>()` function is
also exported (`loadCNV()` is a dispatch function that calls the appropriate one). This
vignette uses FACETS throughout as the single worked example; the
*Parsing CNV caller outputs* vignette shows the individual parsers and the quirks of each
caller's output.

Whichever route is taken, the result is a `cnvstrml` object that contains several slots
with related information
Notably the cnvstrmliner object contains some important slots 
`cnvObj@segments` contains a GRanges object with all the segments and their annotation

The annotation of these GRanges object is uniform and contains the `total.allele.copies`, `major.allele.copies`, 
`minor.allele.copies` etc as well as the `ccf` and `cf` of each segment.
If the method provides subclones (e.g. Battenberg or SCLUST) it also provides the copies of Clone1 and Clone2.

In all cases the column `total.allele.copies` contains the total copies in a segment
`major.allele.copies` the major allele copies and 
`minor.allele.copies` contains the minor allele copies. 
(total.allele.copies = minor.allele.copies + major.allele.copies)
`cnv.loh` is a flag (TRUE/FALSE) indicating if a segment has lost its heterozygosity. 
In combination with the `cnv.annotation` which contains the type of event (NEUT, AMP, DEL, LOH etc) 
it provides a uniform way to annotate segments.
Additionally, when the method provides it the `cnv.cf` and `cnv.ccf` contain the cell fraction (purity)
and cancer cell fraction respectively.
Finally, if the method provides it the logR of the segment is stored in the `cnv.lrr` column.
After qc metrics have been applied the segments also contain the `cnv.cnaqc.pass` flag indicating if the segment passed the CNAqc test or not.


Other slots include `cnvObj@purity` with the purity estimated by the method, 
`cnvObj@ploidy` with the ploidy (which can be a float number) and 
`cnvObj@effective_ploidy` with the ploidy of the majority of the genome (integer)

Several functions exist to plot and analyse the cnv segments either at the sample or group level.
`plotSegments()` gives a visual overview of the genome


## FACETS

For showing the functionality of the package we will start by loading
data produced by the FACETS tool [@facets]. Similarly, other callers can be used
by using the appropriate parser function.


Note that although FACETS is designed to work with matched tumor-normal samples,
cnvstrmliner can also parse FACETS results from unmatched samples. In that case 
the performance of the tool is not guaranteed to be optimal, but combining the calls from
multiple unmatched normals against the same tumor sample (see `ensemblCall()`) can improve
the results.


### Load the CNV calls

Load the FACETS result. We typically expect this in a VCF file
which is provided by the `cnv_facets` pipeline [@cnvfacets].
FACETS is an R package that produces a dataframe with the same information
which can be loaded by handing that data frame to `parseFACETS()` directly.
```{r facets}
# name of the samples for normal and tumor
normal_sample <- "BRCA_XX_01_normal_wg"
tumor_sample <- "BRCA_XX_01_pur30_T"

# location of the example files provided with the package
cnv.fn <- file.path(
  root, "FACETS",
  "BRCA_XX_01_normal_wg-BRCA_XX_01_pur30_T.vcf.gz"
)
# somatic mutations of the tumor sample, used by the QC section below
somatic.fn <- file.path(root, "BRCA_XX_01_pur30_T.somatic-tn.vcf.gz")
has_somatic <- file.exists(somatic.fn)
has_somatic

# parse the FACETS result
# parseCNV() is a dispatch function that calls the appropriate parser synonymous to loadCNV() and readCNV()
cnv <- parseCNV(
  cnv.data = cnv.fn,
  cnv.method = "FACETS",
  sample = tumor_sample,
  genome = "hg38"
)
# or use the FACETS specific function
# cnv <- parseFACETS(cnv.fn, sample = tumor_sample)
cnv
```

### Summary of the object

The function summaryTable() can provide a summary of the main attributes of the cnvstrmliner object
at various levels (genome, chromosome arm) per karyotype.
For more information about the `summaryTable` function see its documentation.

```{r summarytable}
summaryTable(cnv, level = "genome") %>% DT::datatable()

summaryTable(cnv, level = "chromosome") %>% DT::datatable()

summaryTable(cnv, level = "arm") %>% DT::datatable()
```

### Visualize the CNV segments

Let's visualize the CNAs for the whole Genome.
plotSegments() provides a summary plot of the segments called by the method
across all chromosomes.
Arms of the chromosomes are shown in alternating colors for better visibility.
The ploidy of the genome (defined in effective_ploidy slot) is shown as a dashed line.
Green indicates "normal" (normal = ploidy) segments, red amplifications and blue deletions.

For more information about the function `plotSegments` see its documentation.


```{r facets_plot}
plotSegments(cnv)
```

# Working with the parsed object

Everything that follows uses the FACETS object parsed above, but none of it is
FACETS-specific: the same calls work on the output of any supported caller.

## Save the parsed CNV in a VCF file

The parsed object can be saved in a VCF file. This is a rich format that can
contain all the necessary information about the segments and their annotation.
The file contains the standard VCF fields as well as the INFO fields
that describe the CNV segments, and additional INFO fields that are added by cnvstrmliner.


```{r savevcf}
vcf_with_cnvs <- cnvstrmliner::writeVCF(
  cnv,
  filename = file.path(tempdir(), paste0(cnv@sample, "_facets_parsed.vcf.gz"))
)
```

That file can be read back into an equivalent object with `parseVCF()`, which is what the
gene annotation section below does.


## Orthogonal support from structural variants (SVs)

We can try to associate/correlate CNVs with SVs that are predicted by manta.
This will return a new object with the segments flagged with sv.support information.

Manta was not run on `BRCA_XX_01`, so there is no SV call set in the example data and the
chunk below is shown but not executed. Point `manta.fn` at a Manta somatic SV VCF for
your own sample to reproduce it.

```{r manta, eval = FALSE}
sv <- parseManta(manta.fn, sample = tumor_sample)

m <- matchCNVSV(cnv, sv, wiggle = 50000)
m@segments %>% as.data.frame(row.names = NULL)
```

Segments that are supported by the SV method are more likely to be real.
However, even in good samples we expect a concordance of ~70% of the segments 
and in WES this can drop to single digits.


## Annotate using the gene symbols

Using `r Biocpkg("AnnotationHub")` we can get the coordinates of the genes
and annotate the CNV segments wiht them.
This way we can generate custom gene-level reports or segment-level reports
like the one below.

This requires the AnnotationHub and ensembldb packages.
A copy of these commands are provided in the script `annotateGenes.R`
provided with this package. Note that future releases of EnsDb will not be available
through this script.
```{r annotate_segments, cache=TRUE}
library(AnnotationHub)
library(ensembldb)

# load the CNV segments from the VCF we just wrote
cnv <- parseVCF(
  vcf = vcf_with_cnvs,
  sample = tumor_sample,
  genome = "hg38"
)

# Create a connection to AnnotationHub
setAnnotationHubOption("CACHE", "~/AnnotationHub") # set a local cache directory
ah <- AnnotationHub(localHub = dir.exists("~/AnnotationHub"))
# Query for the Ensembl database for Homo sapiens, release 109 (corresponds to hg38)
query_results <- query(ah, c("EnsDb", "Homo sapiens", "109"))
# Load the database
edb <- query_results[[1]]


# Get all genes with their symbols
genes_hg38 <- genes(edb,
  columns = c("gene_name", "gene_id"),
  return.type = "GRanges"
) %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  dplyr::mutate(seqnames = dplyr::case_when(
    seqnames %in% c(seq(1, 22), "X", "Y") ~ paste0("chr", seqnames),
    seqnames == "M" ~ "MT",
    TRUE ~ seqnames
  )) %>%
  makeGRangesFromDataFrame(., keep.extra.columns = TRUE) %>%
  keepStandardChromosomes(., pruning.mode = "coarse")
seqlevels(genes_hg38) <- seqlevels(cnv@segments)


# overlap with the segments
ov <- mergeByOverlaps(
  query = cnv@segments,
  subject = genes_hg38
)

# now show the genes with the annotation of the cnv

subject_ranges <- ov$genes_hg38
chrom <- seqnames(subject_ranges) %>% as.character()
st <- start(subject_ranges)
en <- end(subject_ranges)
ann <- ov[, c("gene_name", "cnv.annotation", "cnv.loh", "cnv.lrr", "cnv.cf", "total.allele.copies", "major.allele.copies", "minor.allele.copies")] %>% as.data.frame()

gene_level <- cbind(
  "sample_id" = cnv@sample,
  "chr" = chrom,
  "start" = st,
  "end" = en,
  "Ploidy" = cnv@effective_ploidy,
  "B.Allele.Freq" = NA,
  ann
) %>%
  dplyr::rename(
    Status = cnv.annotation,
    Ratio = cnv.lrr,
    Absolute.Copy.Number = total.allele.copies,
    Sample.Tumor.Purity = cnv.cf,
    LOH = cnv.loh
  ) %>%
  dplyr::select(chr, start, end, gene_name, Status, Ratio, Absolute.Copy.Number, Sample.Tumor.Purity, LOH) %>%
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(gene_name) & gene_name != "" & Status != "NEUT") %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    chr = stringr::str_remove(chr, "chr"),
    chr = ifelse(chr == "M", "MT", chr),
    Status = dplyr::case_when(
      grepl("NEUT", Status) ~ "Neutral",
      grepl("HOMDEL", Status) ~ "Deep deletion",
      grepl("HETDEL", Status) ~ "Shallow deletion",
      grepl("AMP", Status) ~ "Amplification",
      TRUE ~ Status
    ),
    LOH = dplyr::case_when(
      (LOH == TRUE & Status == "Neutral") ~ "copy-neutral LOH",
      (LOH == TRUE & Status == "Shallow deletion") ~ "LOH: loss of heterozygosity",
      TRUE ~ ""
    )
  )


segment_level <- cnv@segments %>%
  as.data.frame(row.names = NULL) %>%
  dplyr::rename(
    chr = seqnames,
    Status = cnv.annotation,
    Ratio = cnv.lrr,
    Absolute.Copy.Number = total.allele.copies,
    Sample.Tumor.Purity = cnv.cf,
    LOH = cnv.loh
  ) %>%
  dplyr::select(chr, start, end, Status, Ratio, Absolute.Copy.Number, Sample.Tumor.Purity, LOH, major.allele.copies, minor.allele.copies) %>%
  dplyr::filter(Status != "NEUT") %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    chr = stringr::str_remove(chr, "chr"),
    chr = ifelse(chr == "M", "MT", chr),
    Genotype = paste0(
      strrep("A", major.allele.copies),
      strrep("B", minor.allele.copies)
    ),
    Status = dplyr::case_when(
      grepl("NEUT", Status) ~ "Neutral",
      grepl("HOMDEL", Status) ~ "Deep deletion",
      grepl("HETDEL", Status) ~ "Shallow deletion",
      grepl("AMP", Status) ~ "Amplification",
      TRUE ~ Status
    ),
    LOH = dplyr::case_when(
      (LOH == TRUE & Status == "Neutral") ~ "copy-neutral LOH",
      (LOH == TRUE & Status == "Shallow deletion") ~ "LOH: loss of heterozygosity",
      TRUE ~ ""
    )
  ) %>%
  dplyr::select(-c(major.allele.copies, minor.allele.copies))

head(gene_level)
head(segment_level)

data.table::fwrite(
  gene_level,
  file = file.path(tempdir(), paste0(cnv@sample, "-", cnv@method, ".gene_level.tsv")),
  append = FALSE,
  quote = FALSE,
  sep = "\t"
)

data.table::fwrite(
  segment_level,
  file = file.path(tempdir(), paste0(cnv@sample, "-", cnv@method, ".segment_level.tsv")),
  append = FALSE,
  quote = FALSE,
  sep = "\t"
)
```


AnnotSV is a separate application that can be used to annotate
CNAs with the functional elements that are affected.
Typically it expects a .BED file with the corresponding segments.

The utility function `saveAnnotSV` can be used to prepare 
a file that we can use to annotate the segments

```{r annotsv}
annotsv.fn <- file.path(tempdir(), "facets.bed")
saveAnnotSV(cnv, filename = annotsv.fn)
```

Now that file contains the information to run AnnotSV.

`cnvstrmliner` does not provide a direct interface to AnnotSV at this point.


## Export a cohort for GISTIC

GISTIC2.0 identifies the regions that are recurrently amplified or deleted
across a cohort, so it expects the segments of all samples in a single
tab-delimited file. The function `exportGISTIC` produces that file with the
columns `Sample`, `Chromosome`, `Start`, `End`, `Num_Markers` and `Seg.CN`.

`Seg.CN` is the log2 copy ratio relative to the ploidy of each sample,
`log2(total.allele.copies / ploidy)`, using the raw fractional ploidy reported
by the caller. Normalizing by ploidy rather than by 2 means that a
whole-genome-doubled sample does not appear as a genome-wide gain, which keeps
the segment means comparable between samples of different ploidy.

```{r gistic}
gistic.fn <- tempfile(fileext = ".gistic.seg")
exportGISTIC(gistic.fn, cnv)
head(read.delim(gistic.fn))
```

`exportGISTIC` is a preset over `saveSEG`, so the call above is shorthand for
`saveSEG(gistic.fn, cnv, segmean = "ploidy", minSegCN = -5, dropNA = TRUE, style = "gistic")`.
Use `saveSEG` directly if you want a different segment mean — for instance
`segmean = "logR"` with `correct = TRUE` to write purity-corrected log2 ratios
under the same GISTIC column names.

The same call accepts a list of `cnvstrml` objects to build the cohort file,
as long as the sample names are unique:

```{r gistic_cohort, eval = FALSE}
exportGISTIC("cohort.gistic.seg", list(cnv_sample1, cnv_sample2, cnv_sample3))
```

Segments with a total copy number of 0 would give `log2(0) = -Inf`, which GISTIC
cannot parse, so they are floored at `minSegCN` (default `-5`). Note also that
the chromosome names are written exactly as they are stored in the object; most
GISTIC reference files use unprefixed names (`1`, `2`, ..., `X`), so a `chr`
prefix may need to be removed first with
`GenomeInfoDb::seqlevelsStyle(cnv@segments) <- "NCBI"`.


## How purity and subclonality affect the segment mean

The four `segmean` modes of `saveSEG` respond very differently to tumor purity
and to subclonal events, and the choice matters as soon as a cohort mixes
samples of unequal purity.

To see this without depending on a particular caller, we build synthetic samples
where we control the truth. A clone occupying a fraction `CCF` of the *tumor*
cells occupies `cf = purity * CCF` of *all* cells in the sample, so a caller
measuring that segment against a diploid background would report

$$\text{logR}_{observed} = \log_2\left((1 - cf) + cf \cdot \frac{CN}{ploidy}\right)$$

We construct one object per purity, each holding six segments: two and three
total copies, at CCF 1.0 (clonal), 0.6 and 0.3.

```{r purity_grid}
log_threshold(level = WARN, namespace = "cnvstrmliner")

PL <- 2
grid <- expand.grid(ccf = c(1.0, 0.6, 0.3), cn = c(2, 3))

makeSample <- function(purity) {
  cf <- purity * grid$ccf
  lrr <- log2((1 - cf) + cf * grid$cn / PL)
  gr <- GRanges("chr1", IRanges(
    start = seq(1e6, by = 2e6, length.out = nrow(grid)),
    width = 1e6 - 1
  ))
  mcols(gr) <- DataFrame(
    total.allele.copies = grid$cn,
    major.allele.copies = ifelse(grid$cn == 2, 1, 2),
    minor.allele.copies = 1,
    cnv.lrr = lrr,
    cnv.markers = 100L,
    cnv.totalmarkers = 200L,
    cnv.cf = cf
  )
  new("cnvstrml",
    segments = gr, purity = purity, ploidy = PL,
    sample = sprintf("pur%03d", purity * 100),
    genome = "hg38", sex = "F", method = "demo"
  )
}

samples <- lapply(c(0.30, 0.80, 1.00), makeSample)
```

Now write the same cohort out in each mode and collect the sixth column:

```{r purity_grid_table}
segmeanOf <- function(...) {
  f <- tempfile()
  saveSEG(f, samples, ...)
  read.delim(f)$segmean
}

comparison <- do.call(rbind, lapply(samples, function(X) {
  d <- as.data.frame(X@segments, row.names = NULL)
  data.frame(
    purity = X@purity,
    CN = d$total.allele.copies,
    CCF = round(d$cnv.cf / X@purity, 2),
    lrr_observed = round(d$cnv.lrr, 4)
  )
}))

comparison$copies <- segmeanOf()
comparison$ploidy <- segmeanOf(segmean = "ploidy")
comparison$logR <- segmeanOf(logR = TRUE)
comparison$correct <- segmeanOf(logR = TRUE, correct = TRUE)
comparison$correct_usePurity <- segmeanOf(
  logR = TRUE, correct = TRUE, usePurity = TRUE
)

log_threshold(level = INFO, namespace = "cnvstrmliner")
comparison
```

Four things to take from that table.

**Two copies against ploidy 2 is invisible in every log-ratio mode.** Two copies
on a diploid background is no change, so the observed log ratio is 0 at every
purity and every CCF — and a "subclonal" non-event has no meaning. Only
`segmean = "copies"` distinguishes such a segment, by writing `2`.

**Uncorrected `logR` is compressed by purity.** For a single-copy gain it follows
`log2(1 + 0.5 * purity * CCF)`, so a clonal gain reads 0.585 at full purity but
only 0.2016 at 30%. Comparing raw `logR` across samples of differing purity is
not a like-for-like comparison.

**`correct = TRUE` discards subclonality.** It divides by the per-segment
`cnv.cf`, which bundles purity and CCF together, so every three-copy row
collapses to 0.585: a gain carried by 30% of tumor cells is reported identically
to a fully clonal one.

**`correct = TRUE` with `usePurity = TRUE` separates the two effects.** Dividing
by the global purity alone leaves `log2(1 + 0.5 * CCF)`, which depends on CCF but
not on purity. Compare the purity 0.80 / CCF 0.3 row with purity 0.30 / CCF 0.3:
both give 0.2016, even though their raw log ratios differ (0.1635 against 0.0635).
This is the mode to use when subclonality matters.

Note the corollary for `exportGISTIC`: because the `ploidy` mode is derived from
the fitted integer copy number, a subclonal gain is written at full strength and
GISTIC cannot distinguish it from a clonal one. That is the price of being
caller-agnostic and directly comparable across a cohort.


## Perform QC on a sample

First we can compare the expected VAF of somatic events to the observed ones, 
using the `r Githubpkg("caravagnalab/CNAqc")` package.
We need the somatic mutations that have been called on the tumor sample. Internally
cnvstrmliner is using `r Biocpkg("VariantAnnotation")` to load and filter the mutations.
After the function applyQCMetrics finishes the slot cnv@quality$cnaqcobj contains
the results of running CNAqc.
There we can find the `peaks_analysis$QC` and `peaks_analysis$score` for a high level score of the 
cnv quality. A flag == PASS is a good indication that the somatic VAF is within the expected range,
and a score close to 0 means that the predicted purity is very similar to the expected one.
Typically absolute score values  > 0.15 indicate problems with the purity estimation.

The mutations can be handed to `applyQCMetrics` either as a file name or as a data frame
loaded beforehand with `loadMutationsFromVCF()`. That function reads the allelic depths
from the `AD` field of the sample column, so the VCF must carry a sample named exactly as
`cnv@sample` (here `BRCA_XX_01_pur30_T`). It keeps only single-nucleotide substitutions
with a VAF above 0.05 and, with the default `filter = TRUE`, only the calls flagged
`PASS`. Pass `filter = FALSE` to score every record in the file instead — worth doing when
the caller's filters are strict enough that too few mutations survive for CNAqc to fit the
peaks reliably.

The chunks in this section are evaluated only when the somatic call set is present next to
the caller output; otherwise they are shown but skipped, and the CNAqc columns are absent
from the QC table further down.

```{r loadmutations, eval = has_somatic}
mutations <- loadMutationsFromVCF(
  somatic.fn,
  sample = tumor_sample,
  genome = "hg38"
)
nrow(mutations)
head(mutations)
```

Note that the function applyQCMetrics can take advantage of parallelization
using the future package. Here we set a multisession plan with 4 workers.
After the function call we return to the original plan. 
```{r somaticQC, eval = has_somatic, cache=TRUE}
oplan <- plan(multisession, workers = 4) # set parallel processing and keep track of the previous settings
cnv <- cnvstrmliner::applyQCMetrics(
  cnv,
  somatic.mutations = mutations,
  clonal = TRUE, # TRUE is the default anyway
  calculate_chromosome_scores = TRUE # TRUE is the default anyway
)
plan(oplan) # return to the original (probably single thread)

cat(
  "Peak analysis score: ",
  cnv@quality$cnaqcobj$peaks_analysis$score
)

cat(
  "Peak analysis flag: ",
  cnv@quality$cnaqcobj$peaks_analysis$QC
)
```

The score is essentially 0 and the flag is PASS, i.e. the purity that FACETS fitted for
this sample is consistent with the VAF distribution of the somatic mutations.

The applyQCMetrics function can take a long time. One can use the parallelization functions as shown above to speed up the process.
Alternatively set the option calculate_chromosome_scores = FALSE to skip the chromosome level scores and only calculate the overall score.

More detailed information can be obtained from that object if somebody wants to do a more thorough analysis.
Especially the slot `cnv@quality$cnaqcobj$cna` can provide specific information for each segment.
The slot `cnv@quality$cnaqcobj$cna` contains more detailed score per chromosome, however the confidence on this score depends on the number of mutations and is
based on certain, common, karyotypes.
`cnv@quality$cnaqcobj$peaks_analysis$matches` contains a summary of the different common karyotypes
`cnv@quality$cnaqcobj$peaks_analysis$general$summary` contains a summary of the different uncommon karyotypes

The segments are also annotated with the flag `cnv.cnaqc.pass` which indicates if the
segment passed the CNAqc test or not, and `filterLowQualitySegments()` can be used to drop
the ones that did not.

```{r cnaqcpass, eval = has_somatic}
table(cnv@segments$cnv.cnaqc.pass, useNA = "ifany")
```

In addition, we can detect overfragmented chromosomes. 
Typically, unless there is a chromothripsis event overfragmented chromosomes
most likely indicate that the segmentation is not very successfull.

```{r overfragmentation_facets}
cnv <- detectOverfragmentation(cnv, minimum_segments_for_testing = 20)
cnv@quality$fragmentation$table
```


A summary of the QC metrics can be obtained using the qcTable function which returns a data frame with the main QC metrics for the sample.
This is useful if multiple samples are being analysed and one wants to compare them.

```{r qctable}
qc_summary <- qcTable(cnv)
qc_summary
```


An additional metric of the sample's fragmentation is the conditional entropy.
When a cohort of samples is used one can use the whole cohort with the function cnvEntropy() to 
calculate the conditional entropy of all the samples using a common list of shared segments.

To calculate the same metric for a single sample one must first define the segments on the genome.
In a general case one can use the segments that are predicted by the method as is however this is not 
very helpful if one wants to perform some comparison with other samples. For that a common set of segments 
can be defined. For a WES cohort the coordinates of the capture kit are the natural
choice. `BRCA_XX_01` was captured with the Agilent SureSelect Human All Exon V6 kit and
that target file ships with the example data, so we can use it directly.
`cnvEntropy()` accepts either the path of the BED file or an already imported `GRanges`,
and the two are equivalent. Note that due to the number of regions the entropy
calculation may take a long time.

```{r entropy}
exons <- import.bed(bed.file)
length(exons)

cnvEntropy(cnv, bed.file)
cnvEntropy(cnv, exons)
```

Using the capture regions rather than arbitrary windows makes the value comparable across
samples of the same WES cohort, since every sample is scored over exactly the same
intervals.



Everything above used a single FACETS profile. The same functions apply unchanged to
every other supported caller, because all the parsers return the same `cnvstrml`
structure. The *Parsing CNV caller outputs* vignette walks through
Control-FREEC, SCLUST, Sequenza and PureCN on this same sample, and covers
subclones, chromosome-arm annotation, segment-by-segment comparison and
cohort-level consensus.

# Notes 

## Utility functions

`cnvstrmliner::mergeSegments()` : merges adjacent segments of a `GRanges` if they have the
same allele copies. It operates on the `segments` slot and requires the `arm` column, so
run `addChromosomeAnnotation()` first.

```{r mergesegments}
cnv.annot <- addChromosomeAnnotation(cnv)

merged <- cnvstrmliner::mergeSegments(cnv.annot@segments)
length(cnv.annot@segments)
length(merged)
```

`cnvstrmliner::findConsensus()`: finds the common regions between multiple CNV objects  
`cnvstrmliner::addChromosomeAnnotation()`: Adds information about the chromosome arm  
`cnvstrmliner::detectOverfragmentation()`: Detects if a chromosome arm is overfragmented based on the CNAqc algorithm

## Supporting scripts 

Use the `annotateGenes.R` script to annotate the segments with gene symbols

Use the `addCNAqc.R` to load a CNV object and add the CNAqc information to its quality slot

## Cohort analysis

`cnvEntropy()`, `cnvMetrics()`, `findConsensus()` and `plotCNVFreq()` operate on a list of
`cnvstrml` objects rather than on a single sample. They are demonstrated in the
*Parsing CNV caller outputs* vignette, and the agreement metrics themselves in
*Comparing CNV segmentations*.

## Correcting by ploidy and purity

Given the ploidy of genome and its purity The observed log2 ratios are treated as a mix of some fraction of tumor cells (specified by purity), possibly with altered copy number, and a remainder of normal cells with neutral copy number (specified by ploidy for autosomes) by default, diploid autosomes,

Assuming an initial ploidy the various copy numbers (`copies`) are transformed to logR.

$$
logR= log2(copies/ploidy)
$$

However taking the purity (or CCF if we want to be specific for each segment) this transformation becomes

$$
logR=log2( (1 - ccf) + ccf * copies / ploidy )
$$

We can reverse that equation and if we know the CCF we can extract the copy numbers and the set CCF to 1 and recalculate the logR~adjusted~.

$$
logR_{adjusted}=log2( (2^{logR} -(1-ccf))/ccf )
$$


For any given segment we test the above equations.

For each CCF we calculate the logR and then the copy numbers by reversing the logR 
The logR is the "observed" ratio of coverage in log space
The adjusted 
```{r ccf_grid}
ploidy <- 2 # cnvObj@ploidy
copies <- seq(0, 6)
# if we incorporate cff and ploidy
cat("Ploidy        : ", ploidy, "\n")

mat <- lapply(seq(0.1, 1, 0.1), function(ccf) {
  r <- list()
  r["CCF"] <- ccf
  lrr <- log2((1 - ccf) + ccf * copies / ploidy)
  # get back the corrected of copies
  rev_copies <- (2^lrr - (1 - ccf)) * ploidy / ccf
  # recalculate the lrr as if the ccf is 1
  final_lrr <- log2(rev_copies / ploidy)

  r["Real Copies"] <- list(copies)
  r["Reversed calculated"] <- list(round(rev_copies, 0))
  r["logR copies"] <- list(round(lrr, 2))
  r["Adjusted logR (by ploidy)"] <- list(round(final_lrr, 2))

  # OR

  final_lrr2 <- log2((2^lrr - (1 - ccf)) / ccf)
  r["Adjusted logR (using CCF)"] <- list(round(final_lrr2, 2))
  dplyr::bind_rows(r)
}) %>% dplyr::bind_rows()

DT::datatable(mat) %>%
  DT::formatRound(c("Real Copies", "Reversed calculated"), 0) %>%
  DT::formatRound(c("CCF"), 1)
```

we can apply this to a cnvstrmliner object

```{r adjustlrr}
adjustLRR <- function(ploidy, ccf, copies) {
  lrr <- log2((1 - ccf) + ccf * copies / ploidy)
  rev_copies <- (2^lrr - (1 - ccf)) * ploidy / ccf
  log2(rev_copies / ploidy)
}

adjusted.lrr <- adjustLRR(
  ploidy = cnv@ploidy,
  ccf = cnv@segments$cnv.ccf,
  copies = cnv@segments$total.allele.copies
)

head(data.frame(
  copies = cnv@segments$total.allele.copies,
  ccf = round(cnv@segments$cnv.ccf, 3),
  observed.lrr = round(cnv@segments$cnv.lrr, 3),
  adjusted.lrr = round(adjusted.lrr, 3)
))
```

## Logging 

The package is using `r CRANpkg("logger")` for logging purposes.
The logger namespace used for this package is 'cnvstrmliner' for the core functions, 'parser' for the CNV caller parser, 'applyqcmetrics' for the QC metrics 
One can change the level of logging by adding the line `logger::log_threshold(DEBUG,namespace = 'parser')` to show debugging information (or WARN, INFO for higher level annotation)
for the parser actions.
Each logger can be set independently. e.g

```
logger::log_threshold(DEBUG,namespace = 'parser')
logger::log_threshold(WARN,namespace = 'cnvstmliner')
```

## Parallelization

The package is using `r CRANpkg("future")` and `r CRANpkg("future.apply")` whenever possible
To set the number of cores used for parallel processes set the future plan like:

```
oplan <- plan(multisession, workers = 6) # set a parallel processing with 6 cores and keep track of the previous settings for parallelization
# calls to functions of cnvstrmliner
#
plan(oplan) # return to the original (probably single thread)
```
